section.title: Unity in the Body of Christ
section.sectionRationale: This is the pivot of the letter, where the great truths of chapters one to three become a way of life. Having declared what God has done in creating one new humanity in Christ, Paul now urges the church to live it out. The unity of the Spirit is not something believers invent but something they guard, grounded in seven great realities of the one faith. The ascended Christ gives gifted leaders to equip the whole body, so that the church grows to maturity, no longer tossed about by every wind of teaching but growing up into Christ its head, held together in love.
section.thesis: Because there is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all, the church is called to walk worthy of its calling, humbly guarding the unity of the Spirit, while the ascended Christ gives gifted servants to equip the saints so that the whole body, joined to Christ its head, grows up into maturity in truth and love.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the call to walk worthy and keep the unity of the Spirit; the seven ones that ground that unity; grace gifts poured out by the ascended Christ; and the equipping of the saints for maturity as the body grows up into its head.

units.label: Walk worthy: keep the unity of the Spirit

verses.text: As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner {{axios|worthy}} of the calling you have received:
with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
and with diligence to preserve the {{henotes|unity}} of the Spirit through the bond of peace.

units.label: The seven ones
units.note: the ground of the church's unity

verses.text: There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called;
one Lord, one faith, one baptism;
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

units.label: Grace gifts from the ascended Christ
units.note: He ascended and gave gifts to men

verses.text: Now to each one of us grace has been given according to the {{metron|measure}} of the gift of Christ.
This is why it says: "When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men."
What does "He ascended" mean, except that He also descended to the lower parts of the earth?
He who descended is the very One who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.
And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers,

units.label: Equipped for maturity, growing up into the head
units.note: the body builds itself up in love

verses.text: to {{katartismos|equip}} the saints for works of ministry and to {{oikodome|build up}} the body of Christ,
until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ.
Then we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching and by the clever cunning of men in their deceitful scheming.
Instead, {{aletheuo|speaking the truth}} in love, we will in all things grow up into Christ Himself, who is the {{kephale|head}}.
From Him the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part.

axios.gloss: Worthy, fitting, of equal weight, as of a scale balancing evenly. Paul calls the church to a walk that matches the weight of its calling, so that conduct answers to grace. The word does not mean earning the calling but living in a way that fits it, letting the life on the ground correspond to the riches already given in Christ.

henotes.gloss: Oneness, unity. The word appears only here and in verse 13 in the New Testament. The unity of the Spirit is not something the church manufactures but something the Spirit has already created and believers are called to guard diligently, keeping it through the bond of peace rather than fracturing it.

metron.gloss: A measure, a portion measured out, a standard of measurement. Christ apportions grace to each believer according to His own gracious measure, so that no gift is random and none is earned. The same root returns in verse 13, where the goal is the full measure of the stature of Christ, the mature standard toward which the whole body grows.

katartismos.gloss: Equipping, preparing, making fully ready, the mending of what is torn and the setting of what is dislocated. The gifted leaders are given not to do all the work themselves but to make the saints fit for their own works of ministry, so that the whole body is furnished and set in working order for service.

oikodome.gloss: Building up, edification, the act of constructing a house or the structure itself. Paul pictures the church as a building under construction, rising toward completion. The goal of ministry is that the body of Christ is built up, and the same word frames the climax in verse 16, where the body builds itself up in love.

aletheuo.gloss: To speak the truth, to be truthful, to deal truly. The verb carries more than honest words; it is truthing in love, living and speaking according to the truth of the gospel. Set against the deceit and cunning of verse 14, it is the mark of maturity, holding fast to sound teaching while wrapping it in love.

kephale.gloss: Head, both the literal head and, by extension, the source and ruler from which the body draws its life and direction. Christ is the head into whom the church grows and from whom the whole body is supplied and held together. He is both the goal of the church's growth and the origin of its life, the one who governs and nourishes His people.

basic.context: The letter now turns from what God has done to how His people should live. Paul, a prisoner for the Lord, urges the church to live a life that fits its calling: humble, gentle, patient, bearing with one another in love, and eager to guard the unity the Spirit has given. He grounds that unity in seven great realities: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Then he shows that the risen and ascended Christ has poured out grace on each believer and given gifted leaders to the church, not to do all the work alone but to equip every member for service, so the whole body grows up into Christ, its head.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the hinge of Ephesians, where doctrine becomes duty. The word therefore ties the walk of chapters four to six to the wealth of chapters one to three. Read the seven ones as the settled foundation of unity, not a goal to be achieved but a reality to be kept. The gifts of verse 11 are given for the maturing of the whole body, so ministry belongs to all the saints, not only to leaders.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul calls the church to a walk that is axios, worthy, fitting the weight of its calling. Believers are to guard the henotes, the unity, of the Spirit. Grace is given to each according to the metron, the measure, of Christ's gift. Gifted leaders are given for the katartismos, the equipping, of the saints and for the oikodome, the building up, of the body. Maturity means aletheuo, speaking and living the truth in love, as we grow up into Christ, the kephale, the head.
basic.typology: Verse 8 quotes Psalm 68:18, a psalm of God ascending in triumph after victory, and applies it to Christ ascending after His triumph on the cross, distributing the spoils of His victory as gifts to His people. The victorious king who leads captives and gives gifts is fulfilled in Christ, who has conquered sin and death and now equips His church from His throne on high.
basic.christ: Christ stands at the center: He descended and ascended above all the heavens to fill all things, and from His throne He gives grace and gifted servants to His church. He is the measure of the church's maturity, the full stature toward which it grows, and He is the head from whom the whole body is supplied, joined together, and built up in love. The church's unity, growth, and life all flow from Him.
basic.god: God is one, the Father of all, over all and through all and in all, the source of the church's unity. The one God, one Lord, and one Spirit stand behind the seven ones, so that the unity of the church rests on the unity of the triune God. The Father who called His people now sustains and fills them, present in and over the whole body.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12 also picture the church as one body with many gifts given for the common good. Colossians 2 speaks of Christ as the head from whom the whole body grows. Philippians 2 calls believers to the humility and unity Paul urges here.
basic.oneStory: The one new humanity promised through the whole story of Scripture is being built here into a mature body. What sin scattered and divided, Christ gathers and unites, ascending in triumph to pour out gifts and grow His people into Himself. This unity in the Spirit is a foretaste of the day when all things in heaven and earth are gathered up under Christ the head.

context.literary:
Verses 1 to 16 fall into three clear panels, and each turns on a different small word. The first panel, verses 1 to 6, is built on the seven 'ones', and the verb that governs it is a command: preserve the unity. The second, verses 7 to 10, begins with a pivot, 'But to each one of us', and shifts from the One God to the many members, with a quotation from the Psalms to explain how the gifts arrive. The third, verses 11 to 16, is a single long Greek sentence that moves from the gifts to their purpose, the purpose to its goal, the goal to a warning, and the warning to growth. The unity of the first panel and the diversity of the second are brought together in the third, where all the different members build one body.

The seven ones in verses 4 to 6 are arranged in a Trinitarian shape. One Spirit comes first, in verse 4, one Lord in the middle of verse 5, and one God and Father at the end of verse 6, so the list climbs from Spirit through Son to Father, and the Father is the widest, 'over all and through all and in all'. The middle triad, 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism', sits at the centre of the pattern.

A second pattern is a contrast between infancy and maturity. In verse 14 the infant is tossed about by waves and carried by every wind, and in verse 15 the mature body grows up into Christ. The images are of the sea and of the body, one unstable and one stable. The passage ends with 'in love', which is also where verse 2 began, so love brackets the whole section. The 'therefore' of verse 1 links the passage to chapters 1 to 3, and it opens the practical half of the letter, which continues to 6:20.
context.historical:
Paul begins with 'As a prisoner in the Lord'. His authority comes from a chain, not from a position, and the chain gives weight to what he asks. A first century reader would have known that prisoners were commonly held under guard in poor conditions, and the apostle's willingness to describe his state this way shows what he thinks the gospel is worth.

The virtues of verse 2 would have sounded strange in the Greco-Roman world. 'Humility' in Greek writing generally meant something low and servile, with little to admire in it, and Paul uses the word as a mark of Christian character. Gentleness and patience were not the usual virtues of public figures. A church of Jews, Greeks, slaves, free people and women, meeting in homes, needed these qualities, and Paul sets them as the conditions for unity.

The gifts in verses 11 to 12 are people and not abilities. Apostles and prophets have already been named as the foundation in 2:20 and 3:5. Evangelists appear only a few times in the New Testament, such as Philip in Acts 21:8 and Timothy in 2 Timothy 4:5. Pastors and teachers are given to the local congregations, and Acts 20:28 shows elders told to shepherd the flock. The picture is of a young church in which leadership was shaped by the need to teach and to guard.

The warning about waves and winds recalls the world of a port city. Ephesus was a harbour town, and sailors and passengers would know what a boat looked like when it was thrown about. Paul also mentions 'clever cunning', a phrase from dice-play and gambling, which was common in the Roman world. False teachers are like gamblers who cheat.
context.canonical:
The call to unity runs across the New Testament. Jesus prays that His followers may be one, as the Father and Son are one, John 17:20 to 23. Paul pleads with the Corinthians to avoid divisions, 1 Corinthians 1:10 to 13, and to see themselves as one body with many members, 1 Corinthians 12:12 to 27. In Philippians 2:1 to 5 he lists the same virtues, humility, love and being of one mind, and roots them in the example of Christ. Colossians 3:12 to 15 asks believers to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, and places love above them as the bond of perfect unity.

The gifts of verses 7 to 13 belong with Romans 12:3 to 8 and 1 Corinthians 12:4 to 11, 27 to 31, the other lists of gifts. Unlike those lists, Ephesians names persons given to the church and not capacities distributed to members. Paul also uses Psalm 68:18 here, and the text of that psalm is part of the debate on the passage.

The idea of Christ as head and the church as body runs through Ephesians 1:22 to 23 and 5:23, as well as Colossians 1:18 and 2:19. The image of growing up into maturity has a close parallel in 1 Corinthians 14:20 and Hebrews 5:12 to 14. The warning about false teaching is picked up in 2 Timothy 4:3 to 4, which also speaks of itching ears and myths. The picture of the whole body supplied and joined by its parts in verse 16 is close to Colossians 2:19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the church to understand that unity is a gift to be kept, not a project to be built. Everything in the first panel is already true: there is one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God and Father. The church cannot create these. It can only guard them or damage them. So the verb is 'preserve', and the posture it requires is humility, gentleness and patience.

He also wants the church to understand that unity is not uniformity. Grace is given to each one, and the gifts differ. The Ephesians are not to expect everyone to be the same, and they are not to expect a few to do all the work. The leaders in verse 11 are given to equip, and the work of ministry belongs to the whole body. A church that waits for its leaders to do everything has misunderstood the purpose of the gifts.

Third, Paul wants the readers to see maturity as a goal. Unity is paired with growth, and growth with truth and love: 'speaking the truth in love'. A church united but shallow will be tossed about, while one deep in truth but harsh will lose its unity. He wants both together, and he wants them rooted in Christ, who is the head.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1 to 3 are plainly prescriptive: walk worthily, with humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with one another and with diligence to preserve unity. These are commands for all believers in all places.

Verses 4 to 6, the seven ones, are description. They are statements of what is true and are meant to ground the commands. The list is not a creed to be recited, and it is not an exhaustive statement of what must be believed. It names the realities that no Christian can deny without leaving the family.

Verses 7 to 16 mix the two. The account of Christ's ascent and gifts is a description of what He has done, and the list of offices in verse 11 describes what He has given to the church. It would be a mistake to take verse 11 as a rule that every congregation must have precisely these five or that these are the only possible gifts. Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12 list others. What is prescriptive is the purpose in verses 12 to 16: that the saints be equipped for the work of ministry, that the body be built up, that it grow to maturity, and that every part does its share. Whatever structures a church uses, they are measured by this purpose.

debates.question: Psalm 68:18 says God 'received gifts from men'. Why does Paul say He 'gave gifts to men'?

views.label: Paul applies the psalm to its fuller meaning
views.case: The psalm pictures a victorious king returning in triumph, receiving tribute and then distributing the spoil. Paul takes the second part of the pattern: the victor receives and then gives. The conqueror who has received the spoils of victory shares them with His people, as victors in the ancient world did. Acts 2:33 says that Christ received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what the crowd saw, which holds both verbs together.

views.label: Paul adapts the wording to make a point
views.case: The psalm says 'You have received gifts from men, even from the rebellious'. Paul writes 'gave gifts to men', and the BSB footnote suggests the verb can also be read as 'He says'. Some think Paul is paraphrasing, in the way New Testament writers often adapt Old Testament texts to bring out the application. Others think he is giving an interpretation of the psalm as a whole and not quoting it word for word.

debates.bearing: On either reading the thrust is the same: the ascended Christ is the triumphant king who shares the fruits of His victory. The gifts of the church are His spoils, which is why Paul's emphasis falls on His grace and not on human achievement.

debates.question: What does 'descended to the lower parts of the earth' mean?

views.label: The incarnation and death of Christ
views.case: The phrase can be read as 'the lower parts, namely the earth', as a way of saying that Christ came down to the earth in the incarnation. John 3:13 speaks of the One who descended from heaven. Others include His death and burial, so that He went as low as a human being can go, which fits the contrast of verse 10 with ascending above all the heavens.

views.label: Descent into Hades
views.case: Some take the phrase to refer to Christ going to the realm of the dead between death and resurrection, in line with 1 Peter 3:19 and the creedal statement that He descended to the dead. Verse 9 then marks the farthest point down, just as heaven marks the farthest point up.

views.label: The descent of the Spirit at Pentecost
views.case: A smaller group reads the descent as the coming of the Spirit after the ascension, since the gifts are the point of the passage. The wording of verse 10, 'He who descended is the very One who ascended', makes this less likely, because the descent comes first.

debates.bearing: The passage's own purpose helps. Paul is not interested in the geography but in the range of Christ's reach: He has been as low as one can go and as high as one can be, and so there is nowhere He does not fill. All three readings keep that point.

debates.question: Are 'pastors and teachers' one office or two?

views.label: One gift: the pastor-teacher
views.case: In the Greek the first three offices are each introduced by their own 'some', but the last two share one article, so 'pastors and teachers' reads as a single group. On this view the shepherding of a flock is done mainly through teaching, as Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3:2 suggest when they ask overseers to be able to teach.

views.label: Two overlapping gifts
views.case: Others observe that teaching and shepherding are separate in 1 Corinthians 12:28 and Romans 12:7 to 8, and that not every teacher is a pastor. The shared article, they say, shows the two are closely linked and not that they are identical.

debates.bearing: The practical conclusion is the same: those who care for the church must also teach it, and teaching apart from care is not what Paul describes here.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's opening verb is parakaleo, 'I urge', a word with a wide range: to call alongside, to appeal, to encourage and to comfort. It is gentler than a command and warmer than a request, which matches the humility he asks for. He also calls himself desmios, 'prisoner', the same word as in 3:1, so the appeal comes from someone who is bound.

The virtues of verse 2 begin with tapeinophrosyne, 'humility', literally lowliness of mind. Paul pairs it with praotes, 'gentleness', often translated 'meekness', and makrothymia, 'patience', which literally means being long of temper. The latter is used of God's patience with sinners in Romans 2:4 and 9:22, so Christians are being asked to show toward each other what God has shown toward them. Anechomenoi, 'bearing with', is a participle that suggests holding up or putting up with someone, and the phrase 'in love' says in what spirit.

In verse 3 two verbs deserve notice. Spoudazontes, 'with diligence', means to make haste or to be eager. The unity of the Spirit has to be actively guarded. The verb tereo, 'to preserve', means to keep watch over and to guard, which is how it is used for guarding prisoners and treasure. The unity is something already present that must be guarded. The 'bond' is syndesmos, a word for a ligament or a band that holds things together, and it is peace that does the binding. Colossians 3:14 uses the same word for love, the bond of perfect unity, so peace and love are the two ties.

Verse 8 uses the Psalm 68 phrase 'led captives away', which in the Greek is a noun, aichmalosia, captivity, as the object of a verb of leading. It is an image of a conqueror leading a train of defeated enemies, and Colossians 2:15 uses a related picture. In verse 9 'descended to the lower parts of the earth' is expressed with the Greek genitive, which can be read as 'lower parts, that is the earth' or 'lower parts than the earth', and the difference is the substance of the debate.

In verse 11 the grammar of 'pastors and teachers' is notable: poimenas, 'shepherds', and didaskalous, 'teachers', share one article. Poimen is the word for a shepherd, applied to Christ in 1 Peter 2:25.

Verse 13 speaks of the teleios man, the mature one, and the 'full measure of the stature' of Christ. Teleios is used for those who have reached their goal, in contrast to the nepioi, 'infants', of verse 14. Paul then shows the danger of immaturity with two terms for deception: kybeia, 'cunning', the language of dice, and methodeia, 'scheming', from which comes the English 'method'. They describe deliberate tricks.

Finally, the 'supporting ligament' of verse 16 uses haphe and epichoregia. The second word is related to supplying or providing, and in the ancient world it could describe a patron's supply for a chorus. The body is provided for by each joint, and each part contributes, which the final phrase 'the work of each individual part' emphasises.

typology.type: The victor who shares the spoils, Ephesians 4:8
typology.fulfillment: Psalm 68 celebrates God as the divine warrior who ascends the mountain with captives in His train. In the ancient world, a conquering king would receive tribute and distribute gifts to those who shared in the victory. Paul applies this to Christ's ascent after the cross, and Colossians 2:15 describes His triumph over the powers. The escalation is that the spoils are given to the church, not to soldiers, and take the form of people equipped for ministry. The type falls short because earthly victors take plunder from others, whereas Christ gives what costs Him, and the captives He leads are not human prisoners.

typology.type: The body and its members, Ephesians 4:16
typology.fulfillment: Israel was called a people with many tribes joined by one covenant, and the priestly nation was a corporate body under one Lord, Exodus 19:5 to 6. Paul says the church is a single body with one head, Colossians 1:18, and that each part supplies what the whole needs, as in 1 Corinthians 12:12 to 27. The escalation is from a nation bound by descent and law to a body bound by the Spirit and by Christ's life. The picture falls short in the sense that a human body is limited by what it is born with, while the church grows as the Head supplies it and as it adds new members.

typology.type: The journey from infancy to maturity, Ephesians 4:13 to 14
typology.fulfillment: Israel in the wilderness was like a child, unsteady and prone to wander, Numbers 14:2 to 4, and the law acted as a guardian until Christ came, Galatians 3:24 to 25 and 4:1 to 3. Paul pictures the church as moving from the instability of infancy to the stability of adulthood in Christ. The escalation is that maturity is measured by the stature of Christ and not by a code. The picture falls short in the sense that no one in this life fully arrives; Paul writes 'until we all reach', which looks ahead.

typology.type: The gifts of the Spirit for the building of God's house, Ephesians 4:11 to 12
typology.fulfillment: In Exodus 31:1 to 6 and 35:30 to 35 the LORD fills Bezalel and Oholiab with the Spirit and with skill for building the tabernacle, and gives others ability to help. The Spirit equips people for building God's dwelling. Paul says Christ gives leaders to build up His body, which is the true dwelling place, 2:21 to 22. The escalation is from a tent of cloth and gold to a building of living people. The type falls short in that Bezalel's gifts were craft skills, while the gifts here are the people who serve the Word.

study.christ:
The passage begins with the unity of the Spirit and the Father and spends its centre on Christ. The 'one Lord' of verse 5 stands between the Spirit and the Father, and the whole second half of the passage is about what that Lord has done: He descended, He ascended, He gave gifts, and He is the head of the body. Paul wants the church to see that its unity is not just a feeling among members but a person who joins them.

Verses 8 to 10 present a Christ who fills all things. Having gone as low as the earth, and as high as above all the heavens, He leaves no place He has not been and no place He does not reach. The phrase 'in order to fill all things' points back to 1:23, where the church is the fullness of the one who fills everything in every way. John 20:17 gives the first sign of this ascent, when the risen Jesus says He is ascending to His Father and our Father, and Acts 1:9 to 11 records it. The ascent has a purpose: from the throne He pours out the gifts, as Acts 2:33 says.

The gifts are His, and so are the givers: 'it was He who gave some to be apostles'. Leaders in the church are not self-made or elected by the church alone; they are the ascended Christ's own gift to His people. This puts leaders in the position of servants, since they are given to equip and not to rule. It also removes any ground for boasting, as 1 Corinthians 4:7 reminds us.

The final image is of the head and the body. In Colossians 2:19, a person who loses connection to the head cannot grow, and Ephesians 4:15 to 16 says the same positively: from Him the whole body, held together, grows. Christ is not a distant figurehead. He supplies, joins, directs and grows His body. The standard of maturity is Himself, 'the full measure of the stature of Christ', so the question for a church is not whether it is large or impressive but how much it looks like Him.

Notice also the tension Paul holds between the finished and the unfinished. Christ has already ascended and given His gifts, and yet the body is still growing up toward Him. He is already Lord, and the church is still being made like Him. Romans 8:34 says He is at the right hand of God interceding for us, which is the ground of that growth.

A caution against over-reading: the psalm's picture of a warrior king should not be pressed to claim that every detail of Psalm 68 is about Christ. The link is the pattern of triumph followed by distribution, which is enough for Paul's argument.
study.god:
The first thing the passage says about God is that He is one: 'one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.' The three prepositions give a picture of God above creation, working through it and present within it. This is a statement of both transcendence and nearness. He is not one among many gods and not a distant being. The unity of the church is rooted in that oneness, because one God can only have one people.

The passage also shows the Trinity at work in the church. One Spirit, one Lord and one Father are named together, and each acts in the passage: the Spirit gives the unity, Christ gives the gifts, and the Father is over, through and in all. Paul does not write a theory of the Trinity here; he assumes it and builds a practical argument on it. If God is one and three, then the church's unity is not sameness but a unity of persons in relationship, which John 17:21 expresses when Jesus prays that they may be one as the Father is in Him and He is in the Father.

God is also generous. He does not hold back His gifts or give them only to the few. Grace is given to each one of us, according to the measure of Christ's gift. This is a God who is not content to work alone but chooses to build His church through the people He has saved. The gifts are expressions of His character, and they are given through the Son who won them.

God's purposes are patient. The aim of the gifts reaches far beyond the present, 'until we all reach unity in the faith', so God works over a long time and with weak instruments. He allows His people to grow slowly, through the ordinary teaching and love of a congregation, and He does not rush them or give up on them. His patience is the model for the patience He asks of believers in verse 2.

He also cares about truth and love together. The church is to speak the truth in love, and the passage will not let either be sacrificed for the other. A God who is truth does not endorse every wind of teaching, and a God who is love does not make His people hard. Worship that responds to this God is therefore both doctrinally honest and humble toward others. It treats unity as a gift to guard and the truth as a gift to hold, and neither as something to trade away.

crossReferences.note: The psalm that Paul quotes, with the king ascending, leading captives and receiving gifts. Compare 'received' there with 'gave' in Ephesians 4:8. Reading the whole psalm shows a God who rides in triumph and also cares for the fatherless and the lonely, so the ascent is one of victory and generosity.

The risen Jesus is exalted to the right hand of God, receives the promised Holy Spirit from the Father and pours out what the crowd sees and hears. This is the clearest account of the receiving and giving that Paul draws from the psalm, and it shows that the gifts of Ephesians 4 begin at Pentecost.

There are different gifts but the same Spirit, different ministries but the same Lord, different workings but the same God. It shows the same Trinitarian pattern as Ephesians 4:4 to 6, and says each person is given the Spirit's manifestation for the common good.

One body with many members, with different gifts given according to grace. It warns against thinking too highly of oneself and lists gifts of service. It complements Ephesians 4 by showing that the diversity of the body is a matter of grace, not rank.

Paul's appeal for unity rests on humility and on the example of Christ. It names the same virtues, love and being of one mind, and tells believers to consider others more important than themselves. It shows that the ethics of Ephesians 4:2 are patterned on Christ.

Believers are to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, bearing with each other, and to put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity. It is a close parallel to verses 2 and 3 and shows that peace and love are the two ties that hold the body together.

Jesus prays for those who will believe through the apostles' message, that they may all be one as the Father and He are one, so that the world may know that the Father sent Him. It shows that the unity Paul asks the church to guard is also a witness.

Paul pleads with the Corinthians to avoid divisions, and asks, 'Is Christ divided?' It shows what a church looks like when unity is neglected, and why Paul stresses one Lord. The question has an obvious answer, and it exposes the folly of party spirit.

The false teacher has lost connection to the Head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together, grows as God causes it to grow. It is the same picture as Ephesians 4:16, and it reveals what the immature, unstable believer lacks: contact with the Head.

The author rebukes readers who still need milk and not solid food, and says the mature have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil. It illustrates the immaturity Paul describes, and shows that maturity is a matter of discernment trained by constant use.

Paul tells Timothy to preach the word, and warns of a time when people will not tolerate sound doctrine and will gather teachers with itching ears. It is an older Paul looking ahead at the kind of danger that Ephesians 4:14 describes, and it commissions Timothy to do the work of an evangelist.

Spiritual believers restore a person caught in a trespass with gentleness, and carry one another's burdens. It shows what bearing with one another in love looks like in practice, and links it with the law of Christ.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a single human family made in the image of one God, and the first sin breaks it apart. Adam and Eve hide, and then they blame each other. Cain kills Abel. At Babel the nations scatter, Genesis 11:8 to 9. Almost the entire early part of the Bible is a story of division: of one humanity into peoples, of people from God, and of people from one another.

God's response is a call and a promise. He chooses Abraham and promises to bless all families through him, Genesis 12:3. He gathers Israel as one people, gives it one law and one tabernacle, and says through the prophets that He will one day gather the scattered, Ezekiel 37:22 and Isaiah 11:12. Ephesians 4 belongs to that gathering. The one body, one Spirit and one hope are what God promised through the prophets, and what Jesus prayed for in John 17.

The ascension is the hinge that explains how the gathering happens. The Christ who died and rose is exalted, and from His throne He sends the Spirit and gives the gifts. At Pentecost the effect of Babel is reversed, as people from many nations hear the same message in their own languages, Acts 2:5 to 11. The church that results is the first fruit of a restored humanity, and its leaders and members are the means by which that restoration is spread.

The goal is a mature body, described in verse 13 as the full measure of the stature of Christ. This points to the new humanity that began in the second Adam, Romans 5:17 to 19, and the story will not end until it is complete. At the end of the story, Revelation 7:9 sees a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language before the throne, and Revelation 21:3 hears the voice announcing that God will dwell with them. The unity that Paul asks the Ephesians to guard is a small part of the final unity, and every act of humility, gentleness and patience in a congregation is a small sign of it.

quiz.q: What does Paul urge the church to do with the unity of the Spirit?

options.text: To guard and preserve it diligently through the bond of peace.
options.note: Verse 3 calls believers to keep the unity the Spirit has already given.

options.text: To create it themselves through hard effort and organization.
options.note: The unity is the Spirit's gift to be kept, not a human achievement to be manufactured.

options.text: To wait for it to appear once everyone agrees on everything.
options.note: Unity is already given in the Spirit and is guarded now, not postponed until full agreement.

options.text: To abandon it whenever disagreements arise.
options.note: Paul calls for humility, patience, and bearing with one another to keep unity, not to abandon it.

quiz.q: What is the foundation Paul gives for the church's unity in verses 4 to 6?

options.text: The seven ones: one body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, and God and Father.
options.note: The unity of the church rests on these seven great realities of the faith.

options.text: Shared culture, background, and personal preference.
options.note: Paul roots unity in the oneness of God and the faith, not in shared culture.

options.text: A single human leader everyone follows.
options.note: The one Lord is Christ, not a human leader; unity rests on the triune God.

options.text: The absence of any differences among believers.
options.note: Verses 7 and 11 show diverse gifts within a unity grounded in the one God.

quiz.q: According to verses 8 to 10, what did the ascended Christ do?

options.text: He descended, then ascended above all the heavens to fill all things and give gifts.
options.note: Verses 9 and 10 stress the descent and ascent, and the giving of gifts to His people.

options.text: He ascended without ever descending to earth.
options.note: Verse 9 insists that the one who ascended is the one who also descended.

options.text: He received gifts but gave none to the church.
options.note: The citation says He gave gifts to men, the point Paul draws out.

options.text: He remained on earth and sent others in His place.
options.note: He ascended above all the heavens in order to fill all things.

quiz.q: Why did Christ give apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers?

options.text: To equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body.
options.note: Verse 12 names equipping the saints and building up the body as the purpose.

options.text: To do all the ministry themselves while others watch.
options.note: The gifts equip all the saints for ministry, not to replace their service.

options.text: To rule over the church for their own honor.
options.note: They serve the body's growth, not their own status.

options.text: To keep the church divided by rank.
options.note: The gifts are given to bring the body to unity and maturity.

quiz.q: What is the goal of the church's growth in verses 13 to 15?

options.text: Maturity, reaching the full measure of the stature of Christ, no longer tossed about.
options.note: Verse 13 sets maturity in Christ as the goal, and verse 14 the end of being blown about.

options.text: Staying spiritual infants who are easily swayed.
options.note: Paul says we will no longer be infants tossed by every wind of teaching.

options.text: Merely gaining more information for its own sake.
options.note: The goal is maturity and Christlikeness, not information alone.

options.text: Personal success apart from the rest of the body.
options.note: Growth is corporate, the whole body maturing together into Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about Christ as the head in verses 15 and 16?

options.text: The whole body grows up into Him and is held together and built up from Him in love.
options.note: Christ is both the goal of growth and the source from whom the body is supplied.

options.text: The head is separate from the body and gives it nothing.
options.note: From Him the whole body is joined, supplied, and grows.

options.text: Each member grows on its own with no need of the head.
options.note: The body grows from Him, dependent on the head for its life.

options.text: The body holds itself together by its own strength.
options.note: The body builds itself up, yet only as it draws its life from Christ the head.

questions: Paul begins with humility, gentleness, and patience as the marks of a worthy walk. Which of these does the Spirit seem to be pressing on you right now, and where is it hardest to show?
The unity of the Spirit is something to guard, not to create. Where are you tempted to let a relationship in the church fracture, and what would it look like to keep the bond of peace instead?
Christ has given grace to each believer according to His measure. How might God want to use the particular gift He has given you to build up the body?
Verse 12 says leaders are given to equip all the saints for ministry. Do you see ministry as belonging to you, or as something only leaders do, and how might this verse change that?
Maturity means no longer being tossed about by every wind of teaching. What helps you stay anchored in the truth, and where do you feel most vulnerable to being blown off course?
The body grows up into Christ by speaking the truth in love. Where do you find it easier to speak truth without love, or love without truth, and how could you hold them together?

translationNotes.note: This verse quotes Psalm 68:18, a psalm of God ascending in triumph. The psalm speaks of receiving gifts, while Paul says Christ gave gifts to men; he draws out that the victorious king distributes the spoils of his conquest to his people, applying the ascent to the risen Christ.

The lower parts of the earth can be read as the earth itself, so the descent is the incarnation, or as the realm of the dead; either way the contrast is between the depths and the highest heavens, and the point is that the one who descended is the one who ascended.
Pastors and teachers are closely joined in the Greek and may name a single gift, the shepherd who teaches, or two related ministries; both are given for the same purpose of equipping the saints.
